"McInerney should never have worn the CPD star, and it is devastating to accept that he was never identified and held accountable while he was alive. Though her parents have since passed away and were not able to receive justice in their daughter’s murder, we hope that this news brings a measure of closure to all who knew Gloria and her story."

item.title: Americans are secretly cooking during virtual meetings, with one age group leading the way
item.description: A new survey reveals that 17% of remote workers have cooked during video meetings with their cameras off, with Gen Z multitasking at even higher rates. A leadership expert weighs in.
item.content:encoded:
Your colleagues might be chopping, stirring and whipping up a meal on the other side of your video call, a new survey found.

A national survey of more than 2,000 U.S. adults found that 17% of respondents have cooked during a work meeting while their cameras were off — and among Gen Z, the figure rose to 26%.

The poll, conducted by Savanta for AI meeting assistant company Bluedot, also found that 23% have used the restroom during a meeting with their cameras off, 14% have shopped online and 13% have exercised. 

BRINGING THIS POPULAR DRINK TO A JOB INTERVIEW COULD HURT YOUR CHANCES, EXPERTS WARN

Twelve percent, meanwhile, have fallen asleep while their cameras were off, and that figure rose to 30% among Gen Z.

John Coleman, co-CEO of Atlanta-based Sovereign's Capital, told Fox News Digital he has occasionally resorted to eating lunch during back-to-back meetings and taken conference calls while exercising, with his camera off — but he draws the line at cooking while participating in a call.

"I'd hate for someone to have a cooking accident while they're on Zoom and not be a full participant in the meeting," Coleman said.

Some of the other behaviors are even riskier, he noted.

"I had a colleague forget that his video was on and take his laptop into the restroom with him actually — which gave a great view of the restroom to everybody on the call, much to his chagrin," Coleman recalled.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

His tip is to treat video calls — on camera or not — as if you were face-to-face. 

"You want to be engaged with the person across from you," he said. 

For those who need to step away and complete a task, he recommends sending a quick message to let the other people on the call know.

Kristen Hadeed, a Texas-based leadership expert and author of the book "Human Leadership," said her company treats making lunch as "human time" — an everyday need employees should be able to handle. 

"These moments are part of life, and I want my team to feel empowered to take the time they need while maintaining open communication with the team."

She added, "When a person's time away from work will affect their availability, responsiveness or the team's ability to get work done, I expect that it is communicated so that we are all on the same page."

For Catherine Fisher, LinkedIn's vice president of communications and a California-based career expert, the key question is whether multitasking affects someone’s ability to take part.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"The question isn't necessarily, 'Are you doing anything else?' It's, 'Can you still contribute when you’re needed?'" Fisher told Fox News Digital. "If you can't follow the discussion, answer a question or contribute meaningfully, that's when multitasking can start getting in the way of your participation."

Coleman said part of the problem is how some meetings are organized. 

"A lot of this responsibility, I think, rests on organizations," he said. "We overcrowd meetings. We make them too long."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

When employees feel they're not needed in a discussion, or that a meeting could have been handled by email, they may start multitasking, he said — and that erodes cognitive ability. Coleman recommends keeping virtual calls brief, limiting attendance to those who need to participate and asking whether a video call is even necessary in the first place.

Fisher said the higher share of Gen Z respondents who said they've cooked during meetings may reflect how the pandemic shaped their expectations around work and home life.

"I wouldn't look at this data and conclude that Gen Z cares less about work," she said.

"Many started their careers during the pandemic, at a time when the boundaries between work and home had already been rewritten."

item.title: Bears star Caleb Williams could reinjure hamstring by returning too soon, surgeon says
item.description: Chicago Bears star Caleb Williams called his hamstring injury "pretty serious" after feeling a pop, and a surgeon warns rushing back could put him at even greater risk.
item.content:encoded:
Caleb Williams is listed as questionable for the Chicago Bears' game on Sunday against the Atlanta Falcons as he looks to return from his hamstring injury. Should he play, though?

Former college football quarterback-turned-foot-and-ankle surgeon Dr. Drew Burdi isn’t sure if the juice is worth the squeeze. Burdi dealt with a hamstring injury during his playing days at Western Michigan and knows how tough they are to manage.

"I think he could reinjure it," Burdi told OutKick in a recent interview. "I had, when I was playing, I had a hamstring, I pulled my hamstring. It felt the same way. I remember looking around, I was running and I felt like somebody came up and hit me in the back of my leg, and then I realized there was no one around me, and I knew exactly what happened."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Burdi said that when the hamstring is injured, it's actually partially torn. If it's not given time to heal properly, it becomes more susceptible to tearing again.

"Then that just puts stress on other parts of the body, you could be running differently. It can put him in a compromising positions that he just normally wouldn't be in when he's 100%," Burdi said.

Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Williams refused to disclose the medical grade of his hamstring injury but called it "pretty serious."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"I felt a pop," Williams said. "That's why I looked back. I looked back just like everybody else does when you feel a pop. Think somebody grabbed you and nobody grabbed me."

The Bears' star quarterback also said he wasn't sure whether he would play against the Falcons. Burdi said that if Williams has any trepidation, he should sit out another week.

"'Cause they really look good (without him), except for the Packers (game). But I mean, without that game, I don't know. I'd probably say take more time because I think that they could. It depends on their schedule too. If their schedule is good enough where they can get out of it at .500 and have him come back healthy, I think it's better than trying to push himself, win a game, maybe this week, but then he injures it further, and then he might be out longer. It's one of those injuries where you can try to push it, but you really have to know yourself. If it feels like you're still not 100%, it's probably worth just holding off on it," Burdi said.

Without Williams, the Bears have gone 2-1. They beat the Philadelphia Eagles with Case Keenum, beat the New York Jets with Tyson Bagent, and then lost to the Green Bay Packers. Bagent started against the Packers but was replaced by Keenum late in the blowout loss.

If the Bears heed Burdi's advice and sit Williams for one more week if he doesn't feel 100% and lose to the Falcons on Sunday, they will still have managed to go .500 without their star quarterback for a month.

The last thing the Bears need is for Williams to hustle back only to reinjure himself and miss more time.

item.title: The Cignetti effect is real: Indiana football sparks an unbelievable 'revival' in Bloomington
item.description: From Upstairs Pub to Memorial Stadium, Bloomington is electric as Curt Cignetti's Indiana football hosts a historic top-five Ohio State showdown.
item.content:encoded:
The crowd inside the "Upstairs Pub" started to grow as the clock turned toward Friday night on the campus of Indiana, with students getting out of class and heading towards to local drinking establishments for what was going to be a wild 24 hours.

Obviously, the mood has shifted around this college town thanks to the Hoosiers winning last year's CFP title, along with having a head coach in Curt Cignetti who has turned this program into a football juggernaut in just two years.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF IS SACRIFICING ITS SOULD TO BE BECOME AN ATM FOR CONFERENCES WITH 24-TEAM EXPANSION

Whether it was the apparel stores that had fans waiting in lines for their chance to purchase Indiana gear, or the restaurants that were already filling up early Friday afternoon, it's obvious that the attitude has changed around this college town that once glossed over the football season in anticipation for basketball.

Later today, it will be No. 4 Ohio State visiting No. 5 Indiana in what will be the most electric atmosphere Bloomington has seen in decades.

You can call it a "revival," or the Cignetti effect, but it's not hard to notice the culture change in Bloomington.

"We're a football school now, and I hate to say that about the basketball program," Edward, from just outside Indianapolis noted. "We spent years praying for some type of revival of college football within this fan base, and we finally have it during one of the craziest times in sports.

"A lot of schools are trying to pull off the Indiana magic of rebuilding a program in such a short time period. And those expectations are truly centered around what transpired here in Bloomington. That part is wild to me. We expect to win football games now, which is a wonderful feeling to have.

The last time a Hoosiers' football team defeated the Buckeyes in Bloomington was in 1988.

It took thirty years for Indiana to snap a losing streak to Ohio State, which finally came to an end last season inside Lucas Oil Stadium in the Big Ten championship game.

Also, this will be the first time a top-five college football matchup has taken place inside Memorial Stadium since 1960, as Indiana rises a 22-game winning streak into their showdown with the Buckeyes on Saturday.

Essentially, there are a lot of firsts that could end up coming to fruition for an Indiana team that has defied the odds over the past two seasons, against plenty of odds and fans who might still be under the impression this was all just a fluke.

I'm here to tell you that nothing Curt Cignetti is doing on this campus, and opposing ones, is centered around some magical voodoo that the Hoosiers head coach has placed on the Big Ten.

CURT CIGNETTI WAS SO FOCUSED THIS OFFSEASON, HE TURNED DOWN ALL EXTERNAL REQUESTS: 'I'M 95% FOOTBALL'

Whether or not folks outside Bloomington believe Indiana can do it again this season is not the point.

The supporters who are lining Kirkwood avenue, or the thousands who made their way into town on Friday evening, are the true barometer of where this program has been taken in such a short time period that has other college athletic directors trying to replicate the Cignetti magic.

"I don't think folks truly understood what we were going through as a fan base," Thomas, longtime season ticket holder told OutKick. "I've been coming to games for thirty years, and I've never seen this type of excitement, and it's hard to correlate it with basketball. Sure, we're not oblivious to the narrative that followed our football program like a black cloud.

"But, why do you think we're not taking these moments for granted? We've earned this sh-t, and I promise you this fan base isn’t cocky. We just expect to win now, which clearly wasn’t the case just a few years ago. So yea, I expect us to beat Ohio State."

I've been around plenty of college campuses during my career, and the resurgent joy that you see in Bloomington is contagious.

This is no longer a loyal group of fans waiting for November to roll around so they can walk into Assembly Hall to watch the basketball program, which has also had its problems over the years.

But what Indiana football did for the school is provide hope that everything that has transpired over the last two years in one sport, can be done again across multiple venues across campus.

Curt Cignetti has not just provided a championship mindset for the passionate fans that were sitting through days of blowouts and small glimmers of hope in past years.

The man who told you all to 'google' him has reignited an athletic department and fan base that will make Saturday's atmosphere on Indiana's campus feel more like a cinematic backdrop that will host college football's premier matchup of the day.

At the same time, since it's happening here in Bloomington, there are programs across the country that now believe they can pull-off the same type magical story that we're witnessing take place with Indiana.

item.title: Pope Leo XIV discharged from hospital, will return to Vatican after surgery to remove lung cancer
item.description: Pope Leo XIV received blood tests and a chest X-ray at Gemelli Hospital confirming he is well enough to return to the Vatican after surgery.
item.content:encoded:
Thousands of supporters gathered outside Gemelli Hospital in Rome on Saturday after Pope Leo XIV was released following surgery to remove a cancerous node in his lung.

The Holy See announced early Saturday morning that he would be leaving to return to the Vatican.

"Following the doctors’ assessment this morning, Pope Leo XIV will be discharged today from Gemelli Hospital, where he was hospitalized for surgery on his right lung," a statement from the Holy See read.

"He will leave the hospital in the early afternoon and return to the Vatican. Tomorrow, he will lead the Angelus prayer from the window of the papal apartment," the statement added.

The pope received blood tests and a chest X-ray Saturday, both of which confirmed he is well enough to return to the Vatican, according to Vatican News.

Before he departed, Pope Leo reportedly visited the children's oncology ward. While in the hospital, the Pope received letters from some of the children in the ward.

"Pope Leo, our prayers are for you," a girl named Eleonora, who had been receiving treatment in the oncology ward, wrote to him, according to letters released by Vatican News. 

"May God, the Most Holy Virgin, and the guardian angels always protect you," she added. 

Eleanora's mother told the Pope, according to the Vatican, that she was now healthy.

"Faith moves mountains," Eleanora wrote to Pope Leo, adding, "God has heard our prayers."

DR MARC SIEGEL: POPE LEO'S LUNG SURGERY PUTS MODERN MEDICINE ALONGSIDE FAITH

Pope Leo underwent thoracic surgery to remove the node on Tuesday. Following the successful surgery, doctors diagnosed him with lung adenocarcinoma, a form of lung cancer.

"The Pope was in the operating room approximately three hours, while the operation itself lasted about 90 minutes. The doctors said it was successful and there were no complications," a statement from the Holy See press office read.

RECOVERING FROM LUNG SURGERY, POPE LEO URGES PUTIN TO AGREE TO CEASEFIRE IN RUSSIAN-HELD UKRAINE CITY

"Pope Leo awoke normally after surgery and, following a brief period of observation, returned to his room on the hospital’s 10th floor," Vatican News added in a statement.

While recovering, Pope Leo called Russian President Vladimir Putin and urged him to call for a ceasefire in the Ukrainian city of Oleshky.

POPE LEO XIV SEEN FOR FIRST TIME SINCE LUNG CANCER SURGERY AMID MAJOR RECOVERY MILESTONE

"During the conversation, the Holy Father expressed his deep concern about the grave humanitarian situation in the city of Oleshky, in the Kherson region, and called for a ceasefire to allow the delivery of food and medical assistance and the voluntary and safe evacuation of the civilian population," a statement from the Vatican read.

"Finally, the Holy Father reaffirmed the Holy See’s commitment to promoting dialogue and peace," the statement added.

TRUMP WISHES POPE LEO SPEEDY RECOVERY AFTER LUNG CANCER DIAGNOSIS, SPEAKS HIGHLY OF PONTIFF'S BROTHER

Russia has controlled the southern Ukrainian city since May and has not allowed any humanitarian food deliveries in the city. Oleshky also has no electricity, gas or running water, and the hospital is barely functional, according to previous Fox News Digital reporting.

Fox News Digital contacted the Holy See for further comment.

Fox News Digital's Brie Stimson contributed to this report.

Fox News' Courtney Walsh-Annesi contributed to this report.

item.title: MIKE DAVIS: Iowans can't afford a soft-on-crime attorney general
item.description: A University of Iowa College of Law graduate argues Brenna Bird's cold-case murder convictions make her the attorney general Iowa needs reelected.
item.content:encoded:
As an Iowa native, graduate of the University of Iowa and the University of Iowa College of Law, and two-time staffer for Iowa's senior U.S. Senator and Senate Judiciary Chairman Chuck Grassley, I know this for certain: Brenna Bird is the Attorney General Iowa needs reelected. Her Democrat opponent Nate Willems would be a disaster for Iowa, and the choice for voters in November could not be clearer.

Since January 2023, Bird has served with distinction as Iowa's Attorney General. Her credentials are sterling: University of Chicago Law School, years as a prosecutor, county attorney in both Fremont and Guthrie Counties, and president of the Iowa County Attorneys Association — the highest honor a prosecutor can earn in this state. Today, as Iowa's Attorney General, Bird does not merely hold the office. She wields it as a force for justice.

By contrast, Willems has never demonstrated the same seriousness. His legislative record and public conduct reveal a candidate soft on crime, hostile to the Constitution, and willing to smear American heroes for political points. He has no business within a hundred miles of the Iowa attorney general's office.

Consider the results. In 2021, Ryan Cooper, a husband and father in Traer, turned up shot dead in his home. The case sat cold for two years until Bird's newly created cold-case unit took it on. Within months, Karina Cooper and her lover Huston Danker faced arrest. A jury convicted Karina, and she now serves life without parole. Barbara Lenz, a 31-year-old mother in Woodbine, disappeared in 1989 after her abusive partner Robert Davis claimed he dropped her off. No body. No confession. Nearly four decades later, Bird's unit charged Davis. A jury found him guilty, and the judge sentenced him to 50 years. He will never hurt another woman.

That is what a real attorney general looks like.

TRUMP’S PUSH FOR NATIONAL CONCEALED CARRY RECIPROCITY WOULD PROTECT GOOD GUYS WITH GUNS

Willems' record runs the other direction. As a legislator, he voted against requiring electronic monitoring for convicted sex offenders — including those who victimized children. That position disqualifies him on its face. It might fly in San Francisco, but it has no place in Iowa.

His contempt for the Constitution is equally evident. While Bird defends the Second Amendment, Willems voted against making Iowa a shall-issue concealed-carry state — the standard the Supreme Court affirmed as constitutionally required in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen. Willems also seeks to dilute Iowans' voting power by opposing voter-ID laws in a state with two swing House districts and recent races decided by fewer than a dozen votes. And while Bird has filed court briefs supporting federal immigration enforcement, Willems has publicly attacked those policies. A Willems victory would transform Iowa from a legal ally of the president into a state resembling California or Illinois — states dedicated to obstructing federal law enforcement at every turn. Willems does not represent Iowa. He represents the resistance.

WHAT MY SON'S ULTRASOUND TAUGHT ME ABOUT ABORTION — AND MASSACHUSETTS IGNORES

Willems is also an extremist on abortion. He voted against a ban after 20 weeks of pregnancy. Opposing a limit after 20 weeks means defending abortion more than halfway through pregnancy — when the child stands only weeks away from viability outside the womb. That is not moderation. It is a radical position.

Then there is the D-Day post, which should have immediately ended any aspirations Willems harbored of becoming Iowa's top law enforcement officer. On the 82nd anniversary of the Normandy landings, Willems reposted an image equating American paratroopers with leftwing terrorist group Antifa. The caption read: "A plane full of uniformed antifa, circa 1944," placed beside a photograph of the brave American men who jumped behind enemy lines to liberate France from Nazi occupation. Comparing those heroes to an anarchist group responsible for widespread riot violence and attacks on federal officers is not edgy commentary. It is a moral failure. A man willing to smear the heroes of Normandy has no business serving as any state's chief law enforcement officer.

TOP CONSERVATIVE GROUP UNVEILS FULL-COURT PRESS IN KEY BATTLEGROUND STATE TO EXPOSE ‘SHOCKING’ DEM PLATFORM

The contrast for Iowa voters could not be clearer. Bird hunts and prosecutes murderers decades after their crimes; Willems wants convicted sex offenders — including child predators — back on the street without electronic monitoring. Bird defends the Second Amendment. Willems voted to gut it. Bird stands with President Trump. Willems aligns with George Soros. Bird honors the men who died at Normandy. Willems compares them to terrorists. Bird stands with the Constitution and the rule of law. Willems has repeatedly placed ideology above both.

Iowa voters know exactly what they have in Brenna Bird. And they know exactly what they would get in Nate Willems: a radical who is soft on crime.

item.title: Hasan Piker's influence tests breaking point of Democratic Party
item.description: Hasan Piker's Twitch influence is reshaping Democratic Party politics as DSA-aligned candidates gain momentum ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.
item.content:encoded:
Ahead of the midterm elections, one name has repeatedly surfaced in conversations about the future of the Democratic Party: Hasan Piker.

The political commentator streams for hours each day on Twitch, promoting socialism, criticizing Israel and the U.S. and discussing the news of the day from his far-left perspective. But as Piker has gone from a niche online commentator to a real-life player in Democratic politics, his growing involvement has raised questions about what his influence could mean for the future of the party.

While Piker's Twitch streams are viewed by tens of thousands daily, his online reach is not what has drawn the questions about the future of the party; rather, it is how engaged his followers are.

"It's very clear to me that the people who do love and support him, really love and support him. So, the followers that he has are super loyal and I think they're really active, and they're very engaged," Isaac Saul, founder of the non-partisan politics newsletter Tangle, told Fox News Digital.

OCASIO-CORTEZ CALLS FOCUS ON HASAN PIKER 'ABSOLUTELY LUDICROUS' AS SOME DEMOCRATS DEMAND DISTANCE

Piker's followers are mostly young people, a demographic Saul called a "prized possession for the Democratic Party." He explained that Democrats were eager to hold onto young voters "because if they can turn out younger voters, that's going to increase their odds of winning in all manner of elections that happen in American politics."

Mark Penn, a longtime Democratic pollster who served as an adviser to former President Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton, similarly pointed to Piker's appeal to young voters, describing him as almost a "Pied Piper." However, Penn questioned how closely those voters actually align with the streamer's views.

"Nobody could possibly agree with the garbage that Hasan Piker says. It's anti-American, it's antisemitic, it's anti virtually anything, it's anti-having any decorum, sensibility, or intellectual component beyond kind of throwing everything and everyone overboard. So, the whole thing is nihilistic," Penn told Fox News Digital.

STEPHEN A SMITH WARNS HASAN PIKER WILL ‘CONTAMINATE’ DEMOCRATS IN THE MIDTERMS, ‘COME BACK TO HAUNT THEM’

Saul recently outlined his positions on Piker in a piece titled, "My honest thoughts on Hasan Piker." He told Fox News Digital that readers asked him repeatedly, "What's your beef with Hasan Piker?," prompting him to explain his position fully. Saul started his piece by stating that he believes "Piker is a bad guy" and said that he doesn't "trust" the Twitch streamer.

Saul sees Piker as a "big pariah" within the Democratic establishment, even as he gains prominence. The Tangle founder believes, however, that the 2026 midterm elections could shift the party's perspective on Piker and the influence of the far left.

HASAN PIKER VOWS HE WILL PRESSURE JAMES TALARICO TO GOVERN AS A LEFTIST, NOT A MODERATE

"I still view him as kind of an outsider-y person trying to throw his weight around. I think the 2026 midterm has the potential to change that because Piker has endorsed some of the more progressive kind of DSA-type candidates, and if we see them win in House or Senate races, he said, 'We're gonna hold them accountable,'" Saul told Fox News Digital.

Penn also sees the midterms as a potential test of Piker's influence, specifically in the Michigan U.S. Senate race where he was involved with Abdul El-Sayed's campaign. Beyond Piker, Penn sees the midterms as an evaluation of the effectiveness of socialist movements.

"Obviously, I think the Michigan race is a big test case on all of this. I think that if El-Sayed wins in Michigan, then that will be a huge boost to these movements, to people like Piker and all of the outlandishness that they stand for because it wins elections," Penn told Fox News Digital. "If there's a setback here and a setback on the headline elections in Maine, Michigan, and Texas, then maybe the Democrat party is going to come much more to its senses and say these 'movements really didn't work.'"

KYRSTEN SINEMA QUESTIONS WHETHER MODERATES STILL HAVE A PLACE IN THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY

While Saul and Penn see the midterms as a test of whether Piker can leverage his online popularity into real-world results, others argue that the shift is already happening, pointing to the growing number of candidates aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA).

Julian Epstein, a former chief counsel for Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee, told Fox News Digital that he believes mainstream Democrats are underestimating the influence of Piker and the left-leaning movement behind him.

"I think that the lie a lot of moderate Democrats are telling themselves is that you're only going to see 10, 12 members of Congress that fall under the DSA banner, and I think that's delusion," Epstein told Fox News Digital. "I think what you're increasingly seeing is that the socialist movement and the far-left movement is becoming the beating heart of the Democratic Party. Why? Because that's where all the activist energy is, and we saw that with the primaries."

Mainstream and moderate Democrats, according to Epstein, are "scared of this movement" and that they are not willing to fight against it.

"Democrats are increasingly scared to take this movement on because they fear the flying monkeys of the online left," he said.

Epstein also argues that establishment Democrats have lost control of the party. He said Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and other establishment Democrats have ceased being leaders and are increasingly turning into "marionettes of the far-left."

While Epstein believes Piker appeals to "very frustrated" voters who "want to burn down the system," Saul sees some of the streamer's more mainstream views as part of the key to his popularity.

INSIDE HASAN PIKER’S RADICAL VIEWS ON AMERICA, ISRAEL AND SOCIALISM

"Hasan Piker supports Medicare for all. He wants to abolish cash bail. He thinks big agriculture needs to be broken up. He wants to renegotiate our relationship with Saudi Arabia. I mean, I think those ideas are not just broadly popular with progressives, but popular probably with some people in the populist MAGA right," Saul told Fox News Digital. "I think he could become an influential figure. If there was more momentum in Congress to make some of those policy prescriptions law."

As some Democrats attempt to reach Piker's young audience, they could risk losing voters who already feel that the party has gone too far to the left.

JAMES CARVILLE VOWS TO ABANDON DEMOCRATIC PARTY IF FAR-LEFT HASAN PIKER BECOMES LEADING VOICE

Penn noted that political parties could have much more to gain by saying no to extreme movements than going along with them.

"So much time is spent on turnout and base and not enough realization that if I said no to the extremes, I could get a lot of those voters in the middle to switch. And those are twice as powerful as getting those extreme movements," Penn said.

Tanya Tsikanovsky, a former Democrat who worked to elect Hillary Clinton in 2016 before later leaving the party, told Fox News Digital that she believes the Democratic Party's shift to the left is leaving voters like her politically "homeless."

"I think that we need to stop focusing on how bad or how maybe salvageable the Democratic Party is and not think about them at all, and instead focus on the independents or on the moderate Democrats, like I once was, that feel completely homeless," Tsikanovsky told Fox News Digital. "Because there are a ton of [Sen. John] Fettermans and Bill Mahers that are gonna really not have anywhere to go soon. Their party is going to be completely eaten up by the DSA."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Tsikanovsky agreed with Epstein's assessment that moderates in the Democratic Party have been left without power amid the rise of DSA candidates across the country.

"The DSA candidates and people like Hasan Piker are the ones that are being platformed by that party and the moderate ones don't really have power anymore at all," Tsikanovsky said.

The debate over Piker's role in the Democratic Party is at the heart of a larger question about how far left the party is willing to shift in order to gain voters, and how much that change could cost or benefit them.

Saul argued that Piker's influence is best understood by viewing his ability to shape the national conversation, rather than seeing him as a politician or activist.

"I think when you consume his content, or you think about him as a player in the space, you should think about them as a kind of provocateur, a pundit. Not a journalist, not even an activist. Not a politician, but somebody who is just trying to change the conversation culturally that people are having. And I think, when you do that, he makes a lot more sense," Saul said.

Fox News Digital reached out to Hasan Piker and the DSA for comment.
